item.content:encoded:
Author: Jessiely Consolacion

In Part 1 of this series, Running Agent Substrate on VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service, we demonstrated how to package and deploy Agent Substrate as a VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) add-on. Agent Substrate solves the low-level runtime problem: it schedules sandboxed Actors onto warm worker pools, isolates untrusted execution with gVisor, and suspends idle workloads via sub-second state snapshots.

Once you have a hardened, high-density runtime running on your VKS clusters, platform teams still face the upper-stack challenge: how do you declaratively define what those agents do, connect them to enterprise tools, govern LLM credentials, and coordinate multi-agent workflows across teams?

Running an AI agent in isolation is relatively simple; managing fleets of agents consistently across enterprise teams is where platform architectures are tested. As organizations move beyond individual agent deployments, they need a standardized, Kubernetes-native way to define agent behavior, govern model access, enforce tool permissions, and coordinate multi-agent orchestration.

Enter kagent—an open-source CNCF project that brings declarative, Kubernetes-native management to AI agents. In the architecture explored in this series, kagent complements Agent Substrate by providing an orchestration layer for defining agent behavior, configuring model access, and managing interactions with enterprise tools, while Agent Substrate provides the underlying execution runtime.

As the second step in a broader series on enterprise agentic architectures on VKS, this post bridges runtime primitives and full end-to-end workflows (which we’ll explore further in Part 3 and beyond) across four areas:

  • Layering kagent onto Agent Substrate to turn sandboxes into governed agents
  • Packaging kagent as a composable VKS add-on that consumes your Agent Substrate runtime
  • Installing the kagent add-on on Substrate-enabled VKS workload clusters via the VCF Automation UI or declarative GitOps

From Low-Level Actors to Declarative Agents

In our Agent Substrate post, we worked directly with low-level runtime primitives—scheduling individual Actors onto worker pods and verifying gVisor isolation and cross-worker snapshot resumption. While essential for infrastructure engineering, application teams shouldn’t have to manage raw Actor lifecycles or manually wire up model endpoints and tool servers for every agent they build.

Figure 1: Declarative Agent Orchestration with kagent

kagent bridges this gap by introducing Kubernetes custom resources that compile down into workloads scheduled on your existing Agent Substrate worker pools:

  • Agent and AgentTemplate: Separate what an agent does (system prompts, skills, sub-agents, and tool allowlists) from its runtime configuration, letting teams reuse standardized agent behaviors across environments.
  • Harness: Connects an agent definition to the underlying Agent Substrate execution engine—binding kagent’s Go/Python ADK, Claude, Codex, or custom runtimes directly to the Substrate worker pools provisioned by your base add-on.
  • ModelConfig: Centralizes LLM provider configurations (Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, Bedrock, Ollama, or internal AI gateways) and injects credentials at egress so raw API keys never sit inside the agent sandbox.
  • RemoteMCPServer and MCPServer: Connects agents to external enterprise systems and built-in Kubernetes/infrastructure toolsets over the Model Context Protocol (MCP) with per-agent tool allowlists.

Together, kagent’s controller, web UI, PostgreSQL session store, and OpenTelemetry tracing wrap Agent Substrate’s Actor model in a complete, GitOps-friendly platform.

Orchestration Meets Execution: The Request Flow

When an alert or user request triggers concurrent work across several agents, kagent and Agent Substrate divide execution cleanly:

  1. On-Demand Session Dispatch: kagent coordinates task delegation over the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol, routes tool calls over MCP, and requests sandboxed Actor instances on demand from your pre-warmed Agent Substrate worker pool. Each active session runs securely inside a gVisor sandbox.
  2. Turn Boundary: The Actor stops executing the moment it reaches a turn boundary and requires external input to proceed including an LLM response, a Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) approval click, or a new user prompt. 
  3. Suspension and Snapshot: The Actor is immediately suspended. Process memory is discarded, and its current state (including the filesystem and pending workflow state) is snapshotted to durable object storage rather than being kept “warm” in memory.
  4. Worker Release: Because the Actor is suspended to object storage, the compute Worker pod is immediately freed to handle other tasks. This reduces idle compute consumption, allowing available worker capacity to be reused for other agent workloads.
  5. Sub-Second Restoration: When the LLM responds, or when a human finally replies or clicks approve, kagent retrieves the snapshot. Agent Substrate boots a container on whichever warm Worker pod has capacity and restores the snapshot in milliseconds, resuming the Actor precisely where it left off to process the input.

Zero Application-Level Hooks Required: In the kagent implementation, suspension and resumption are automatic and managed by the underlying runtime infrastructure. You do not need to write explicit application-level hooks, state-saving logic, or “suspend” API calls into your agent’s code; the runtime triggers suspension at every turn boundary as soon as nothing in the session is actively running.

Packaging kagent as a Composable VKS Add-on

Note: While VKS supports add-on extensibility, the specific add-on manifests and artifacts referenced in this post are intended solely for demonstration. These examples are not officially supported production configurations. Detailed packaging mechanics for VKS add-ons are still evolving and will be covered in a future post in this series. You can learn more about VKS add-ons in the Managing Add-ons in VKS Clusters documentation.

One of the biggest advantages of the VKS add-on framework is modularity. Instead of building a monolithic package that overwrites or duplicates the Agent Substrate add-on from our first post, we keep Agent Substrate and kagent as two distinct, composable VKS add-ons to ensure:

  • Independent Lifecycle and Ownership: Infrastructure teams can tune worker pool sizing, update gVisor, or upgrade the node-level atelet daemon via the agent-substrate add-on without disrupting the kagent control plane—and AI platform teams can roll out new kagent features independently.
  • Shared Runtime Density: A single Agent Substrate add-on deployment can serve as a shared, multi-tenant execution fabric for kagent (as well as any custom internal Actor workloads), maximizing worker pool utilization across the cluster.

When layered onto a Substrate-enabled VKS cluster, the kagent add-on integrates cleanly across four touchpoints:

  1. Control-Plane-Only Footprint: Rather than spinning up duplicate worker pods, the kagent add-on deploys strictly the orchestration layer—the kagent controller, web UI, and built-in MCP server—delegating all sandboxed execution to your existing Agent Substrate runtime.
  2. Direct Runtime Binding: Through AddonConfig, you point kagent to the local Agent Substrate control plane endpoint. Default Harness definitions then automatically target the warm, gVisor-isolated worker pools already managed by your base add-on.
  3. Fleet-Wide Guardrails out of the Box: Platform administrators can pre-populate cluster-wide defaults—including approved ModelConfig LLM gateways, OIDC authentication, private container registry mirrors, and egress network policies—so application teams inherit enterprise governance from day one.
  4. Coordinated CAPI Lifecycle Management: Because VKS tracks compatibility constraints and reconciles add-ons alongside Cluster API (CAPI), both the agent-substrate and kagent add-ons benefit from drift self-healing and validated, non-disruptive upgrades across your fleet.

Installing the kagent Add-on on VKS

Assuming your target VKS workload clusters already have the agent-substrate ClusterAddon deployed and reporting Ready (as covered in the previous post), layering on kagent follows the exact same VKS workflow:

  • Via the VCF Automation UI: Navigate to the VKS Cluster Management add-ons catalog in VMware Cloud Foundation Automation, select the kagent add-on, point it to the cluster’s existing Agent Substrate runtime and default LLM gateways, and deploy onto your target VKS clusters.
  • Via GitOps and kubectl: Declare an AddonInstall using label selectors or CEL constraints to target clusters already equipped with the Agent Substrate add-on, pair it with a per-cluster AddonConfig, and monitor rollout progress through the ClusterAddon status resource.

Once ClusterAddon transitions to Ready, the kagent control plane is online and ready to compile Agent definitions into ActorTemplates—spinning up sandboxed agent sessions on demand across your cluster’s pre-warmed Substrate worker pools whenever requests arrive. 

Advancing the Kubernetes-Native Agentic Stack on VKS

As enterprises move from AI agent experimentation toward broader adoption, platform teams need more than the ability to run individual agents. They need a consistent foundation that allows them to manage, govern, and evolve AI agent workloads without tightly coupling every layer of the architecture.

The modular approach explored throughout this series illustrates how VKS can provide that foundation:

  • VKS and the Add-on Framework provide consistent infrastructure provisioning and lifecycle management across Kubernetes environments on vSphere.
  • Agent Substrate provides a shared execution foundation designed for isolated, resource-efficient agent workloads.
  • kagent introduces declarative agent management and orchestration, bringing agent definitions, model access, and tool configuration into Kubernetes-native workflows.

By separating infrastructure, execution, and orchestration, enterprises can evolve these layers independently, establish clearer operational responsibilities, and incorporate emerging cloud-native AI capabilities as their requirements change.

This is where the extensibility of VKS becomes particularly valuable. Rather than prescribing a single, monolithic AI agent stack, VKS provides a foundation on which platform teams can compose architectures that reflect their organization’s evolving needs.

In Part 3, we’ll build on this architectural foundation with a practical reference pattern demonstrating how agent definitions, multi-agent orchestration, MCP governance, and end-to-end workflows come together.

Ready to dive deeper? Revisit Part 1, Running Agent Substrate on VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service, to learn how the underlying runtime add-on is constructed and configured. You can also watch Solo.io’s Introducing kagent: Managing AI Agents in Kubernetes to explore kagent’s declarative orchestration and observability capabilities in action.

item.content:encoded:
VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) Operations checks my lab against its compliance rules and shows me what has drifted. That’s fine in the UI, but I wanted to do the same from a script: pick one setting, check it, fix it, check again. In VCF 9.1 that work is done by Salt, and Salt comes with an API, the VMware Salt for VCF Components API. This post is what I worked out while using it to fix NTP on six ESX hosts. Some of it is in the docs. Some of it I had to dig out of the job history.

By the end you’ll have:

  • A bearer token for the API
  • A few read-only calls to look around (minions, Salt environments, files, and jobs)
  • An NTP spec for ESX, drafted with a community generator and pushed to the Salt file server
  • An assessment and a remediation run against the ESX hosts behind a vCenter

Where this API fits

The configuration compliance side of VCF, Security Posture Management (SPM) in VCF Operations, is powered by Salt. When VCF Operations assesses your environment, it doesn’t log in to vCenter or NSX itself. It sends Salt jobs to a RaaS server and Salt minions running on the VCF components perform assessment and remediation. The Salt for VCF Components API is the API of that RaaS server, so whatever SPM does, you can do yourself.

A few things that helped me get a picture of it:

  • RaaS runs as pods in the VSP Kubernetes cluster, in the salt-raas namespace. You reach it through the fleet LCM FQDN at /raas/rpc. The docs write this as https://<vcfms-hostname>/raas/rpc; in my lab it is fleetlcm.gpu.set.lab.
  • Minions run on the components themselves: vCenter, the NSX Managers, SDDC Manager, the VCF Operations nodes, and the cloud proxy, plus one minion pod inside VSP.
  • ESX hosts have no minions. The vCenter minion checks and fixes them through vCenter. That decides how you target everything later.
  • The compliance content lives in a Salt environment called vcfsecops, not in the usual base.
  • The nightly assessment is a state.apply of a state called ops_assess_u, with a pillar that specifies which objects to check and the desired values. You can read those jobs using the API, and that was the most useful thing I found.

Authentication

There are three hops: an API token from VCF Operations, an exchange at the VCF instance’s Identity Broker (vIDB) for a bearer token, and then providing that bearer token on every RaaS call.

1. Create an API client in VCF Operations

Prerequisite: VCF SSO must be enabled and configured before you can generate an API token.

In VCF Operations go to Manage > Fleet Management > Identity and Access > Identity Broker > API Access. Create an API client with the Config Admin role (VCF Administrator includes it by default), then generate a token in the UI and copy it. It starts with vidb_. Treat it like a password.

2. Exchange it for a bearer token

The vIDB token endpoint takes the API token with a custom grant type and hands back an OAuth access token:

export VIDB=vidb.gpu.set.lab
export RAAS=fleetlcm.gpu.set.lab
export VIDB_API_TOKEN='vidb_...'

TOKEN=$(curl -sk -X POST "https://$VIDB/acs/t/CUSTOMER/token" 
        -H 'Accept: application/json;charset=UTF-8' 
        -H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' 
        --data grant_type=urn:custom:vcf:params:oauth:grant-type:api-token 
        --data-urlencode "api_token=$VIDB_API_TOKEN" | jq -r .access_token)

CUSTOMER in the path is the tenant, and it worked as-is for me. The access token is short-lived, so when calls start failing on auth, run the exchange again. I use -k only because my lab runs on self-signed certificates.

3. Call RaaS

Every call is a POST to /raas/rpc with a JSON body that names a resource, a method, and its keyword arguments. A small shell helper saves a lot of typing:

raas() {
  curl -sk -X POST "https://$RAAS/raas/rpc" 
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" 
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" 
    -H "Accept: application/json" 
    -d "$1"
}

Pass it a JSON string, or @file.json to send a file. The response always has the same envelope:

{ "riq": 216948794121888, "ret": { "...": "..." }, "error": null, "warnings": [] }

ret holds the result and error tells you what went wrong. These are the error codes I ran into:

For a 5000, or when calls just hang, the RaaS logs tell you what happened. I ran these on a VSP node:

kubectl -n salt-raas get pods
kubectl -n salt-raas logs -f {raas-pod} --tail=100

I also keep all of these calls in a VS Code REST Client file, which is nicer for clicking through responses. The token request gets a name, and the other requests reuse its result:

### Get bearer token
# @name gettoken
POST https://{{vidbFqdn}}/acs/t/CUSTOMER/token
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=urn:custom:vcf:params:oauth:grant-type:api-token&api_token={{vidbApiToken}}

###
@token = {{gettoken.response.body.access_token}}

The whole REST Client file is in the GitHub repo for this post:
https://github.com/denysaleksandrov/vfc-salt-api-test

Looking around

Before changing anything, I want to know what’s connected, which files are on the Salt side, and what has been running. All of the calls in this section are read-only.

Which minions are present

Presence shows which minions are connected, with the minion ID next to the host name:

raas '{"resource":"minions","method":"get_minion_presence","kwarg":{"status":"present"}}' 
  | jq -r '.ret.results[] | [.host, .minion, .status] | @tsv'

salt-minion-55cd4df7db-w84lj  ed35318e-0da5-43a1-95bb-a692eaaf1272  present
nsx03                         00c4b75e-97bb-4e39-928c-5c55190ae3cd  present
ops02                         3e539c47-06b9-4527-97f0-746053059bb6  present
ops01                         e2e0da68-5036-410e-b01d-cd5ece515828  present
vc01                          349eea8d-e7c8-47f6-b2ea-a197ea245562  present
collector                     97805429-66a3-474e-bdc6-08b28def8a70  present
sddcm                         e6b92638-46a8-4bc2-a6b2-e8ad19defbf3  present
nsx04                         a94ac790-0d99-4d0f-a251-85b76496b9a5  present
ops03                         9d93bcf7-fc2f-4a97-970e-24c04a675b66  present
nsx02                         b85d6a5f-b0ba-464f-b3c4-680fa00e8702  present

ret.get_minions lists the minion IDs grouped by Salt master:

raas '{"resource":"ret","method":"get_minions"}' | jq .ret
{

  "salt-master-5d1353b8-aa1a-463d-b00c-eeb680f93b0e": [
    "a94ac790-0d99-4d0f-a251-85b76496b9a5",
    "9d93bcf7-fc2f-4a97-970e-24c04a675b66",
    "b85d6a5f-b0ba-464f-b3c4-680fa00e8702",
    "ed35318e-0da5-43a1-95bb-a692eaaf1272",
    "00c4b75e-97bb-4e39-928c-5c55190ae3cd",
    "3e539c47-06b9-4527-97f0-746053059bb6",
    "e2e0da68-5036-410e-b01d-cd5ece515828",
    "349eea8d-e7c8-47f6-b2ea-a197ea245562",
    "97805429-66a3-474e-bdc6-08b28def8a70",
    "e6b92638-46a8-4bc2-a6b2-e8ad19defbf3"
  ]
}

minions.get_minion_details returns the grains of every minion when you call it without arguments. Two grains matter most here: fqdn, and vcfops_resource_kind, which says what the component is:

raas '{"resource":"minions","method":"get_minion_details","kwarg":{}}' 
  | jq -r '.ret.results[] | [.id, .grains.vcfops_resource_kind, .grains.fqdn] | @tsv'

00c4b75e-97bb-4e39-928c-5c55190ae3cd  nsxm         nsx03.gpu.set.lab
349eea8d-e7c8-47f6-b2ea-a197ea245562  vcenter      vc01.gpu.set.lab
3e539c47-06b9-4527-97f0-746053059bb6  ops          ops02.gpu.set.lab
97805429-66a3-474e-bdc6-08b28def8a70  cloud-proxy  collector.gpu.set.lab
9d93bcf7-fc2f-4a97-970e-24c04a675b66  ops          ops03.gpu.set.lab
a94ac790-0d99-4d0f-a251-85b76496b9a5  nsxm         nsx04.gpu.set.lab
b85d6a5f-b0ba-464f-b3c4-680fa00e8702  nsxm         nsx02.gpu.set.lab
e2e0da68-5036-410e-b01d-cd5ece515828  ops          ops01.gpu.set.lab
e6b92638-46a8-4bc2-a6b2-e8ad19defbf3  sddcm        sddcm.gpu.set.lab
ed35318e-0da5-43a1-95bb-a692eaaf1272  vmsp         salt-minion-55cd4df7db-w84lj

You can also filter on a grain, and list the values a grain has across all minions:

raas '{"resource":"minions","method":"get_minion_details",
       "kwarg":{"grains":{"vcfops_resource_kind":"vcenter"}}}' 
  | jq -r '.ret.results[] | [.id, .grains.fqdn] | @tsv'

raas '{"resource":"minions","method":"get_minion_grain_values",
       "kwarg":{"key":"vcfops_resource_kind"}}' | jq -c .ret

In my lab the kinds are vcenter, nsxm, ops, sddcm, cloud-proxy and vmsp. No ESX hosts, as expected.

Salt environments and files

raas '{"resource":"fs","method":"get_envs"}' | jq .ret

On my system that returns ["vcfsecops"]. To list the files in it:

raas '{"resource":"fs","method":"get_env","kwarg":{"saltenv":"vcfsecops"}}' 
 | jq -r '.ret[] | [.path, .content_type] | @tsv'
/_utils/nsxt_edge.py     text/plain
/_utils/esxi.py          text/plain
/ops_assess_u.sls        application/x-yaml
/ops_remed_u.sls         application/x-yaml
/_utils/cp.py            text/plain
/_utils/vro.py           text/plain
/_utils/vra.py           text/plain
/_utils/hcx.py           text/plain
/_utils/vcenter.py       text/plain
/_utils/sddc_manager.py  text/plain
/_utils/nsxt_manager.py  text/plain
/_utils/avi.py           text/plain
/_utils/ls.py            text/plain
/_states/ops.py          text/plain

You’ll see ops_assess_u.sls, ops_remed_u.sls, _states/ops.py and a set of _utils/*.py files, one per product. To read a file use fs.get_file. The contents come back base64-encoded unless the file was stored as text/plain:

raas '{"resource":"fs","method":"get_file",
       "kwarg":{"saltenv":"vcfsecops","path":"/ops_assess_u.sls"}}' 
 | jq -r .ret.contents | base64 -d

That’s the state VCF Operations applies for its assessments, and it’s worth reading:

{% set saltenv="vcfsecops" %}
{% do salt["saltutil.sync_all"](saltenv=saltenv, refresh=True) %}
install_config_modules:
  ops.pkg_install:
    - saltenv: {{saltenv}}
{% set minion_id = grains['id'] %}
{% set ids = pillar['object_id'][minion_id] %}
{% set object_type = pillar.get("object_type") %}
{% set target_control_config = pillar.get("desired_spec") %}
compliance_{{object_type}}:
  vmware_compliance_control.check_control:
    - control_config: {{ target_control_config | tojson | safe }}
    - product: {{ object_type }}
    {% if object_type in ["esxi", "vm", "nsxt_edge"] %}
    - ids: {{ ids }}
    {% endif %}
    - require:
      - install_config_modules

It syncs the custom modules from vcfsecops, installs the config-modules package where a product needs one, and then calls vmware_compliance_control.check_control. 

Everything comes from the pillar: object_type, object_id and desired_spec. For ESX, VMs and NSX Edges it also passes ids, the list of objects to check. On my build ops_remed_u.sls is the same file. Whether it only assesses or also fixes comes down to Salt’s test flag, as you’ll see below.

Jobs

There are a few ways to look at jobs, and they show different things. job.get_jobs lists saved job definitions. Mine is empty, because VCF Operations doesn’t save its jobs there:

raas '{"resource":"job","method":"get_jobs","kwarg":{}}'  jq .ret

The job history lives under ret.get_jids gives the recent job IDs with the function and the user, and get_jid gives the per-minion return of one job:

raas '{"resource":"ret","method":"get_jids","kwarg":{"limit":"50"}}' 
  | jq -r '.ret | to_entries[] | [.key, .value.fun, .value.user] | @tsv'

20261112154759893040 state.apply             master_salt-master-5d1353b8-aa1a-463d-b00c-eeb680f93b0e
20261112154759878819 state.apply             master_salt-master-5d1353b8-aa1a-463d-b00c-eeb680f93b0e
20261112154759864913 state.apply             master_salt-master-5d1353b8-aa1a-463d-b00c-eeb680f93b0e
20261112154759849769 state.apply             master_salt-master-5d1353b8-aa1a-463d-b00c-eeb680f93b0e
20261112154759830857 state.apply             master_salt-master-5d1353b8-aa1a-463d-b00c-eeb680f93b0e
20261112154759815920 state.apply             master_salt-master-5d1353b8-aa1a-463d-b00c-eeb680f93b0e
20261112154759797240 state.apply             master_salt-master-5d1353b8-aa1a-463d-b00c-eeb680f93b0e
20261112154732417375 saltutil.refresh_grains master_salt-master-5d1353b8-aa1a-463d-b00c-eeb680f93b0e
20261112153232155513 saltutil.refresh_grains master_salt-master-5d1353b8-aa1a-463d-b00c-eeb680f93b0e
…

Pick a JID from that list to see what each minion returned:

raas '{"resource":"ret","method":"get_jid","kwarg":{"jid":"20261112010353733411"}}' | jq .

Then there’s ret.get_returns, which is the one I’d point anyone to first. Filter on state.apply and every result includes fun_args, which is the exact pillar VCF Operations sent: object type, object IDs and the full desired spec.

raas '{"resource":"ret","method":"get_returns","kwarg":{"fun":"state.apply","limit":50}}' 
  | jq -c '.ret.results[]
  | {jid, type: .fun_args[1].pillar.object_type?, ids: .fun_args[1].pillar.object_id?}'

{"jid":"20261112154759893040","type":"vrops","ids": {
"3e539c47-06b9-4527-97f0-746053059bb6":["3e539c47-06b9-4527-97f0-746053059bb6"],
"9d93bcf7-fc2f-4a97-970e-24c04a675b66":["9d93bcf7-fc2f-4a97-970e-24c04a675b66"],
"e2e0da68-5036-410e-b01d-cd5ece515828":["e2e0da68-5036-410e-b01d-cd5ece515828"]}}

Whenever I wasn’t sure what a call should look like, I found the job VCF Operations ran for the same object type and copied it.

Finding the IDs you need

Two kinds of ID go into every compliance call for ESX: the vCenter minion ID and one or more ESX host IDs. I got both wrong at least once, so here’s where they come from.

The vCenter minion ID

Minion IDs are UUIDs, not host names. In my lab, the vCenter minion ID is the same value as its vcfops_resource_id grain. The quickest way to find it is the grain filter from the previous section, which gives one line per vCenter:

349eea8d-e7c8-47f6-b2ea-a197ea245562   vc01.gpu.set.lab

It’s used in two places:

  • as the target of the job: "tgt": {"*": {"tgt": "L@<vcenter-minion-id>", "tgt_type": "compound"}},
  • as the key of the pillar’s object_id map, with the ESX hosts as its value.

Because object_id is a map, one call can cover several vCenters: one key per vCenter minion, each with its own list of hosts. The state looks up its own minion ID in that map, so every minion you target needs a key there.

ESX host IDs

This is where I lost the most time. My first guess was the managed object ID from the vCenter URL, host-25 for esx214. The assessment came back with an overall COMPLIANT and I was pleased for about a minute, until I looked at the per-host result:

"host-25": {
  "errors": ["Host 'host-25' is not managed by this vCenter."],
  "status": "SKIPPED"
}

For ESX, the IDs are the host names as vCenter and VCF Operations know them. In my lab those are the FQDNs, esx213.set.lab to esx218.set.lab. VMs are different again: for them VCF Operations sends managed object IDs like vm-31. The quickest way to get the host list is, once more, a job VCF Operations already ran:

raas '{"resource":"ret","method":"get_returns","kwarg":{"fun":"state.apply","limit":50}}' 
  | jq -c '[.ret.results[] | select(.fun_args[1].pillar.object_type? == "esxi")]
  | max_by(.fun_args[1].pillar.desired_spec.compliance_config.esxi | length)
  | .fun_args[1].pillar.object_id'

{"349eea8d-e7c8-47f6-b2ea-a197ea245562":[
 "esx213.set.lab",
 "esx214.set.lab",
 "esx215.set.lab",
 "esx216.set.lab",
 "esx217.set.lab",
 "esx218.set.lab"]}

(The max_by picks the job with the most settings in its spec, so it’s one of VCF Operations’ runs and not one of your own test runs.)

Also note that a skipped host doesn’t fail the run. Always read the per-host status, not only the summary.

What VCF Operations sends per object type

Here’s what I found in the job history for each object type, in case you want to go beyond ESX. The grain kind and the object type don’t always use the same name.

Drafting the NTP spec

For the desired values I used the Salt for VCF Component State & Jinja File Generator from Salt for VCF github page. You pick a component, pick configuration IDs from a list and fill in the values, and it gives you a Salt state file and a Jinja file with the settings. It saved me a lot of digging, mostly because it lists every configuration ID per component with its title and a sensible starting value.

For ESX, NTP is three configuration IDs:

  • 147: ESX host must configure NTP time synchronization.
  • 148: The ESX host must configure NTP Service startup policy.
  • 149: Start NTP service on the ESX host.

I started with 147 alone and two NTP servers.

Before pushing, I changed two names, so the spec matches what the compliance module expects. It is also the shape VCF Operations sends:

  1. The top-level key. The generator uses state_to_jinja_linked_name as the link between the state and the Jinja file. check_control wants compliance_config there, with the product (esxi) one level below it. With any other name the run ends with Desired spec is empty or not in correct format.
  2. The setting name. The module has its own names for settings, and the one for 147 is ntp_config. The easiest place to find them is a VCF Operations assessment job:
raas '{"resource":"ret","method":"get_returns","kwarg":{"fun":"state.apply","limit":50}}' 
  | jq -r '[.ret.results[] | select(.fun_args[1].pillar.object_type? == "esxi")]
  | max_by(.fun_args[1].pillar.desired_spec.compliance_config.esxi | length)
  | .fun_args[1].pillar.desired_spec.compliance_config.esxi
  | to_entries[] 
  | [.value.metadata.configuration_id, .key, (.value.value | tojson)] 
  | @tsv'

For NTP, that gives these names. The values are the ones I want:

protocol is required for ntp_config. If you leave it out, the host reports a validation error. The generator already fills it in.

Here are the two files I ended up with. The Jinja file holds the spec:

{# Save this file to: esx_component.jinja #}

{% load_yaml as global %}
compliance_config:
  esxi:
    ntp_config:
      metadata:
        configuration_id: "147"
        configuration_title: "ESX host must configure NTP time synchronization."
      value:
        protocol: "ntp"
        servers:
          - "10.3.0.10"
          - "10.3.1.10"
{% endload %} {# Required for Salt to process Jinja file properly. #}

The state file loads it and passes it to the compliance check:

{% set esx_component_config = "compliance_config" %}

{% from 'esx_component.jinja' import global with context %} #Insert the path location where your jinja file is located
{% set control_config = global[esx_component_config] %}

{% set target_control_config = {"compliance_config": control_config } %}

esx_component_settings:
  vmware_compliance_control.check_control:
    - control_config: {{ target_control_config }}
    - product: "esxi"

Push the files

Files go to the Salt file server with fs.save_file. The docs say text files can be sent as plain text, but my build base64-decodes whatever arrives in contents. A plain-text upload got me a 5000 and a binascii.Error in the RaaS log. So I base64-encode everything:

push() {   # push {local file} {path in vcfsecops}
  raas "$(jq -nc --arg p "$2" --arg c "$(base64 < "$1" | tr -d 'n')" 
    '{resource:"fs", method:"save_file",
      kwarg:{saltenv:"vcfsecops", path:$p, contents:$c}}')"
}

push esx_component.jinja /esx_component.jinja
push esx_ntp.sls /esx_ntp.sls

raas '{"resource":"fs","method":"get_env","kwarg":{"saltenv":"vcfsecops"}}' 
  | jq -r '.ret[] | [.path, .content_type] | @tsv'

…
/esx_component.jinja
/esx_ntp.sls

Assess

For the actual run, I went back to the built-in states, ops_assess_u and ops_remed_u, and passed my spec through the pillar, the same way VCF Operations does. The generated state doesn’t pass ids, which ESX needs. The Jinja file is still where I keep the spec; yq turns its YAML into the JSON for the pillar:

VC_MINION=349eea8d-e7c8-47f6-b2ea-a197ea245562
ESX_HOSTS='["esx213.set.lab","esx214.set.lab","esx215.set.lab",
            "esx216.set.lab","esx217.set.lab","esx218.set.lab"]'

# the YAML inside the Jinja file, minus the Jinja lines, is the desired spec
SPEC=$(sed '/^{[%#]/d' esx_component.jinja | yq -o=json -I=0 '.')

jq -n --arg vc "$VC_MINION" --argjson hosts "$ESX_HOSTS" --argjson spec "$SPEC" '
{
  resource: "cmd", method: "route_cmd",
  kwarg: {
    cmd: "local", fun: "state.apply",
    arg: { arg: ["ops_assess_u"],
           kwarg: { saltenv: "vcfsecops", test: true, queue: true,
                    pillar: { object_type: "esxi",
                              object_id: { ($vc): $hosts },
                              desired_spec: $spec } } },
    tgt: { "*": { tgt: ("L@" + $vc), tgt_type: "compound" } }
  }
}' | tee esx_ntp_assess.json

If you’d rather not use jq, this is the request it builds (host list shortened):

{
  "resource": "cmd",
  "method": "route_cmd",
  "kwarg": {
    "cmd": "local",
    "fun": "state.apply",
    "arg": {
      "arg": ["ops_assess_u"],
      "kwarg": {
        "saltenv": "vcfsecops",
        "test": true,
        "queue": true,
        "pillar": {
          "object_type": "esxi",
          "object_id": {
            "349eea8d-e7c8-47f6-b2ea-a197ea245562": ["esx213.set.lab", "esx214.set.lab", "..."]
          },
          "desired_spec": {
            "compliance_config": {
              "esxi": {
                "ntp_config": {
                  "value": { "protocol": "ntp", "servers": ["10.3.0.10", "10.3.1.10"] },
                  "metadata": {
                    "configuration_id": "147",
                    "configuration_title": "ESX host must configure NTP time synchronization."
                  }
                }
              }
            }
          }
        }
      }
    },
    "tgt": { "*": { "tgt": "L@349eea8d-e7c8-47f6-b2ea-a197ea245562", "tgt_type": "compound" } }
  }
}

A few things in there:

  • test: true is Salt’s dry run, so check_control only reports.
  • queue: true queues the run if another state run is already going on the minion, which can happen while VCF Operations is doing its own.
  • object_id maps the vCenter minion to its ESX hosts, and tgt sends the job to that same minion.

Send it, wait a little, and fetch the return:

JID=$(raas @esx_ntp_assess.json | jq -r .ret)
sleep 10
raas '{"resource":"ret","method":"get_jid","kwarg":{"jid":"'"$JID"'"}}' | tee assess_result.json

The return is long. These two filters give the per-host status and the NTP details:

jq '.ret[].return[] | select(.__id__=="compliance_esxi")
    | .changes | del(.metadata_grains) | map_values(.status)' assess_result.json

jq '.ret[].return[] | select(.__id__=="compliance_esxi")
    | .changes | del(.metadata_grains)
    | map_values(.host_changes.compliance_config.esxi.ntp_config)' assess_result.json

All six came back NON_COMPLIANT, and for esx214 the second filter showed exactly what I expected, one server configured and two wanted:

{
  "esx213.set.lab": "NON_COMPLIANT",
  "esx214.set.lab": "NON_COMPLIANT",
  "esx215.set.lab": "NON_COMPLIANT",
  "esx216.set.lab": "NON_COMPLIANT",
  "esx217.set.lab": "NON_COMPLIANT",
  "esx218.set.lab": "NON_COMPLIANT"
}
…
"esx214.set.lab": {
  "status": "NON_COMPLIANT",
  "current": { "servers": ["10.3.0.10"] },
  "desired": { "servers": ["10.3.0.10", "10.3.1.10"] }
}

The state itself reports result: null, which is Salt’s way of saying “this would change” in test mode.

Remediate

Remediation is the same request with ops_remed_u and without test. Run the assessment first and read it, because this one changes your hosts.

jq '.kwarg.arg.arg = ["ops_remed_u"] | del(.kwarg.arg.kwarg.test)' 
 esx_ntp_assess.json | tee esx_ntp_remediate.json

JID=$(raas @esx_ntp_remediate.json | jq -r .ret)
sleep 10
raas '{"resource":"ret","method":"get_jid","kwarg":{"jid":"'"$JID"'"}}' | tee remediate_result.json

The same two filters, run on remediate_result.json, show SUCCESS for all six hosts and the server list before and after:

{
  "esx213.set.lab": "SUCCESS",
  "esx214.set.lab": "SUCCESS",
  "esx215.set.lab": "SUCCESS",
  "esx216.set.lab": "SUCCESS",
  "esx217.set.lab": "SUCCESS",
  "esx218.set.lab": "SUCCESS"
}
…
"esx214.set.lab": {
  "new": { "servers": ["10.3.0.10", "10.3.1.10"] },
  "old": { "servers": ["10.3.0.10"] },
  "status": "SUCCESS"
}

In vCenter, esx214 now lists both servers and the NTP service is running.

Finally, run the assessment again. Every host should come back COMPLIANT for ntp_config.

Things that tripped me up

  • A skipped host still gives an overall COMPLIANT. Read the per-host status.
  • ESX IDs are host names (FQDNs in my lab), not host-NNN. VM IDs, on the other hand, are vm-NNN.
  • The files live in vcfsecops. Pass saltenv to state.apply, or Salt looks in base.
  • On my build, fs.save_file wanted base64 for .jinja and .sls files.
  • Setting names are fixed by the module (ntp_config, not ntp). Copy them from a VCF Operations job.
  • The API docs follow the latest release. On my build, tgt.get_tgts, test.ping and stats.get_stats return 3001. The upload and run snippet on the generator page uses fs.write_file and job.run, while my build has fs.save_file and cmd.route_cmd. Check what yours has; a 3004 means the method is there.
  • Grain kinds and object types use different names (nsxm and nsxt_manager, ops and vrops).
  • When something returns 5000, the RaaS pod log has the real error.

What’s next

Next I’ll add 148 and 149 to the same spec, so the NTP service is set to start with the host and is running, and then work through the other ESX settings that come back non-compliant. 

Because object_id is a map, the same request will cover more than one vCenter once there’s a second one in the lab.

References

  • Security Posture Management, VCF 9.1 documentation on Broadcom TechDocs
  • From Open Source to Enterprise: Understanding the VMware Salt API Evolution
  • VMware Salt for VCF Components API on the Broadcom Developer Portal, in particular the minions, fs, cmd, ret, job and tgt interfaces
  • Salt for VCF Component State & Jinja File Generator (9.1.1)
  • REST Client for VS Code
  • GitHub repo for this post: https://github.com/denysaleksandrov/vfc-salt-api-test

item.content:encoded:
Thousands of remote sites keep business moving, often without a single systems administrator on site. That gap creates the defining challenge of the distributed edge: heavy hardware sprawl run by a lean team. VMware Cloud Foundation Edge (VCF Edge) is an optimized configuration of VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) built for edge use cases. It runs traditional VMs, native containers, and edge AI workloads on one consistent platform across thousands of remote locations, with centralized policy and automation doing the heavy lifting.

Following the release of VCF Edge 9.1, we are continuing to build on that foundation by delivering new capabilities for VCF Edge in 9.1.2 for fleet management, application delivery, and security to improve operations. Here’s what’s new in these releases, and what it means for running edge sites.

Edge Fleet Operations: AI Diagnostics, Compliance, and Kubernetes Upgrades

Operating thousands of distributed sites requires a single management view. These releases take a step toward that goal.

AI-powered diagnostics speed up root-cause analysis. The VCF AI Assistant within VCF Operations, introduced Tech Preview, brings conversational, AI-driven diagnostics. Technicians can ask questions to accelerate root-cause analysis across thousands of edge sites, without needing specialized expertise. Cross-site anomaly detection correlates real-time health signals to catch cluster instability and fleet-wide patterns before they cause downtime, and unified fleet health visibility automatically distinguishes an isolated site failure from a systemic issue. The result, lower mean time to repair (MTTR) reducing late night fire drills for lean IT team. 

Compliance at scale, from a single console. VCF Edge now supports fleet-scale compliance and remediation across VCF components, automating ongoing checks against PCI DSS 4.0 and VMware Cloud Foundation security baselines for thousands of remote sites in one view. Distributed operators and retailers can detect configuration drift centrally and pull compliance reports in minutes rather than weeks, reducing manual work for regional staff and store teams.

VCF Operations dashboard interface showing a compliance assessment 

Chained Kubernetes upgrades give lagging fleets a predictable path. In VMware vSphere Kubernetes Services (VKS) 3.8, automated chained version upgrades orchestrate a cluster from an older Kubernetes version automatically figuring out the intermediate upgrade steps needed to move to the target version, with no manual dependency mapping. The system automatically applies the latest stable patch at each step and keeps add-ons synchronized with the platform version, so fleets that have fallen behind can catch up with a predictable, low-risk path. For sites that are air-gapped or disconnected, the new VKS Upgrade Planner, released via GitHub, identifies the exact stable intermediate patch releases needed to prepare local repositories before an upgrade ever touches production.

Kubernetes and Edge AI at Edge Sites with VKS. VKS Quickstart removes the “empty box” friction that slows Kubernetes adoption at remote sites. Built natively into vCenter, it walks platform teams through a simple three-step workflow to activate the vSphere Supervisor, deploy Harbor, and deploy a VKS cluster, delivering Day 1 readiness for app development without specialized onsite IT or external automation tools. Available in VCF 9.1.2, VKS Quickstart also pre-integrates essential add-ons and a visual UI like Headlamp, allowing application teams to deploy and test edge AI and modern workloads right away.  

A harder target for attackers. Platform hardening in VKS 3.8 programmatically disables Secure Shell (SSH) across Kubernetes control plane and worker nodes, closing a common entry point for brute-force attacks and eliminating manual, error-prone OS-level configuration. For edge sites such as retail storefronts, branch offices, and factory floors, or in any environment with limited physical perimeter security, that is a meaningfully smaller attack surface by design.

Edge Security: Confidential Computing and HyperArmor

When hardware runs outside locked cages and without local IT support, attackers look for easy openings, stolen passwords, unpatched hosts, and exposed ports.

Confidential computing protects data in use. Hardware-isolated workloads, supported through AMD Secured Encrypted Virtualization-Secure Nested Paging (SEV-SNP) and Intel Trusted Domain Extension (TDX), encrypt data while it’s actively processing in memory and isolate workloads from the host. Now natively integrated into the VCF Edge platform, confidential computing protects data, so even if an edge device or hypervisor is compromised, sensitive data and regulated workloads stay protected extending zero-trust principles all the way to the edge. VCF Operations identifies which ESX hosts can run confidential VMs and containers, and Quick Boot is supported on hosts with confidential computing active, which helps keep maintenance windows short.

Hardware isolated confidential computing security boundary

Proactive defense at the hypervisor layer. VMware HyperArmor¹ is a new software solution to help further protect the VMware ESX hypervisor component of VCF against sophisticated cyber attacks.  It delivers host-layer, real-time virtual patching that mitigates exploit attempts without a host reboot, giving IT teams room to plan and apply permanent patches on their own schedule. HyperArmor also continuously monitors the ESX hypervisor and blocks suspicious behavior, and it adds multi-factor authentication to SSH, so a stolen password alone does not grant access. Together, these help protect business continuity against rapidly increasing threats.

VMware HyperArmor sits between VMs and ESX to provide proactive threat defense.

One Edge Platform for VMs, Containers, and AI at Every Site

With VCF Edge 9.1.2, distributed organizations can manage thousands of remote locations in a single view, deploy modern apps and Edge AI workloads without specialized on site IT, and harden physically exposed infrastructure. Operators run VMs, containers, and AI workloads consistently across one, two, or three-plus node sites, from the core data center to the farthest edge.

Ready to see VCF Edge in action? Explore the resources below or talk to your Broadcom representative.

item.content:encoded:
Introduction

While artificial intelligence offers transformative potential, enterprise deployment remains constrained. At the forefront, privacy, IP protection, and compliance present severe existential threats. Foundational issues however are infrastructural demands—such as GPU bottlenecks, network I/O, and compute expenses—forcing a delicate trade-off between high-performance execution and sustainable spending. Every AI project starts in the same place: Day-0. Before a single workload runs, IT teams have to line up compute, storage, networking, and Kubernetes runtimes. It is complex, it takes time, and it is where good AI plans often stall.

Per IDC:

  • Complexity slows production. 73% of respondents agree that AI infrastructure complexity delays moving from proof-of-concept to production. *
  • Performance is next. 42% believe AI inference and performance will be a top operational challenge over the next two years.*

Announcement – AI infrastructure quickstart

To solve the challenges of infrastructure complexity, Broadcom announces general availability of the AI infrastructure quickstart in VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) 9.1.2. This feature automates Day-0 setup, replacing a time-consuming, multi-step process with a streamlined guided workflow delivered through a VMware vCenter plugin.

AI infrastructure quickstart is built for enterprise environments, including air-gapped and connected AI workloads. It brings together three steps that teams have historically handled separately: vCenter cluster configuration, VMware vSphere® Supervisor activation, and VMware vSphere® Kubernetes Service cluster setup.

Key Benefits

The AI infrastructure quickstart offers several benefits to enterprises:

  • Streamline AI infrastructure deployment: The quickstart replaces complex, multi-step manual configuration across compute, storage, networking, and Kubernetes with a single, coordinated workflow.
  • Accelerate time-to-value: Faster deployment helps move AI workloads from POC to production sooner, by eliminating setup delays and operational bottlenecks.

Real-World Impact: What Our Customers Are Saying

Enterprises across industries are already deploying AI services in VCF solving the challenges of infrastructure complexity of their AI workloads:

“Private AI was an accelerator for discovery for us. From the very first deployment of AI services in VCF, we had a basic proof of concept of a chatbot running within a couple of hours, the same day. That let us put experimentation in the hands of the whole team. Today, our teams are building their own agents with AI Services in VCF. One of them handles Level 1 triage on incoming alerts, correlating context and proposing next steps, so the team can keep up with the volume without adding headcount. Our #1 driver for embracing VCF 9 was the vision of a truly unified private cloud platform that could handle all our workloads. “

– Mark Fournier, CIO/CTO, United States Senate Federal Credit Union  

Feature Details

Let’s get into the details. 

  1. Software Defined Data Center (SDDC) Cluster Bring-Up: This step creates the clusters  with GPU-enabled hosts.

  • VMware components automatically enabled: VMware vSphere High Availability (HA) and VMware Distributed Resource Scheduler (DRS) are automatically enabled.
  • Host Selection: Compatible hosts are automatically selected and presented.
  • Distributed Switch and Storage Setup are streamlined in this step.
  1. Supervisor Activation: This step gets the VMware vSphere Supervisor deployed on the vCenter cluster and the namespace ready.

  • Air-gapped or connected AI workload selection: Selection can be made here by admin for air-gapped or connected workloads.
  • GPU VM Classes: Ready-to-use GPU VM classes scaling up to 128 vCPUs are automatically created.
  • Network setup: Management network for the control plane VMs and the network your workloads run on are easily created.
  • Load Balancer Integration: FLB (Foundation Load Balancer) or Avi (NSX Advanced Load Balancer) options are provided.
  • Container Registry Deployment: Bring your own container registry selection for air-gapped AI workloads.
  1. VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) Cluster Deployment

In this final step, a VKS cluster is set up and NVIDIA tools and drivers are installed.

  • NVIDIA tools and drivers:
    • NVIDIA Network Operator, NVIDIA Data Center GPU Manager (DCGM) and NVIDIA GPU Operator are required and installed by default. 
    • NVIDIA Run:ai is optional and can also be deployed through the same workflow.

Want to know more? 

  • Visit VMware.com/AIML for more information. 
  • Connect with us on Twitter at @VMwareVCF and on LinkedIn at VMware VCF.

*Source: IDC Tech Buyer, C-Suite Strategies to Maximize AI Factory Business Benefits, #US54819826, August 2026.

item.content:encoded:
Infrastructure teams don’t get to choose when a new threat emerges or when a support ticket lands at the worst possible moment. What they can choose is how prepared their platform is to respond. VMware vSphere Foundation 9.1 set out to modernize infrastructure economics by cutting operational downtime and unlocking superior performance. VMware vSphere Foundation 9.1.2 builds directly on that foundation, adding targeted capabilities that strengthen hypervisor security, simplify day-to-day operations, and accelerate Kubernetes adoption, without asking IT teams to change how they already work.

This is an incremental release by design. Rather than a sweeping overhaul, 9.1.2 delivers a small set of high-value capabilities that address specific friction points customers raised: proactive defense against fast-moving threats, faster support resolution, and a smoother path to production Kubernetes.

Defend the hypervisor against emerging threats 

AI-accelerated threats move faster than traditional patch cycles, and the hypervisor is too central to infrastructure to leave exposed while a permanent fix is tested and staged. VMware HyperArmor adds a proactive layer of defense to protect the VMware ESX hypervisor component of VMware vSphere Foundation and close that exposure window without disrupting workloads.

Host-layer virtual patching mitigates exploit attempts within the host nodes before vulnerabilities can be exploited, without requiring host reboots or software upgrades, giving IT teams operational flexibility to test and apply official patches on their own schedule. Positive security guardrails establish a known-good baseline for continuous monitoring and automatically block unauthorized executables or scripts at the infrastructure layer, while hypervisor-level multi-factor authentication (MFA) integrated directly into the ESX SSH login path ensures a stolen root password alone is no longer enough to reach the command line. Together, these capabilities help protect business continuity, reduce risk windows, and neutralize credential-based attacks.

Simplify operations with smarter diagnostics

Troubleshooting a high-availability failover should not require piecing together information from multiple places. VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) Operations now gives administrators Supervisor cluster-level diagnostics for vCenter HA events, with visibility that reduces the time to root cause. Log Assist generates and attaches comprehensive support bundles, including vSphere Supervisor, core services, VMware ESX, and vCenter logs, directly to support cases, cutting out a step that used to slow down every support engagement. Configurable capacity management cool-down periods prevent unecessary resizing recommendations by giving the system a defined window between adjustments, so capacity planning reflects real trends rather than feedback noise.

Accelerate Kubernetes ecosystem adoption

Platform teams want to give developers fast, flexible access to Kubernetes without taking on unpredictable support relationships, and they want to spend less time managing infrastructure. With VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) 3.7, the Add-on Management Framework broadens the choice of ecosystem tools with predictable support ownership.

Deployment itself is faster too. VKS Quick Start accelerates time to value by deploying a production-ready VKS cluster, so developers can start building on Day 1. Platform teams can quickly enable the vSphere Supervisor with a guided workflow and start running Kubernetes workloads. Teams can also deploy essential add-ons and use the intuitive GUI to visualize clusters and resources for rapid workload testing.

Many organizations struggle to keep pace with rapid Kubernetes release cycles and continuous open-source innovation. VKS 3.8 introduces automated chained upgrades that determine feasibility, orchestrate upgrades from an older version to the target version, and select the latest stable patch at each step. The result is shorter maintenance windows and lower risk of upgrade failures along the way.

Built for continuity, not disruption

VMware HyperArmor, the VCF Operations diagnostics enhancements, and the VKS 3.7 Add-on Management Framework extend the same core priorities that shaped VMware vSphere Foundation 9.1: lower operational burden, stronger security posture, and faster time to value. Built directly in response to feedback from customers running VMware vSphere Foundation in production, these updates deliver faster threat response, faster support resolution, and faster time to a working Kubernetes environment, all without requiring you to rearchitect existing infrastructure or disrupt workflows. item.content:encoded:
VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) 9.1.2 brings native S3-compatible object storage to vSAN. Block, file, and object are all a part of the vSAN component of VMware Cloud Foundation, so infrastructure teams can use their existing investments in vSAN to support cloud-native apps and AI workloads with S3-compatible object storage. The capability ships with the VCF license, runs on the vSAN hardware customers already own, and gives developers self-service bucket provisioning with multi-tenancy from day one through VCF Automation.

IT leaders consolidating their storage footprint get a third storage type as an integrated platform feature instead of another silo to manage. For IT decision makers, that means one less appliance to procure, power, and operate. For administrators, it means one management plane instead of two or three.

Why On-Premises Object Storage is Now a Requirement
Since the vast majority of data created today is unstructured, file and object storage will see robust demand growth going forward. Cloud-native applications and AI projects, both experiencing significant growth, are large users of object storage. Broadcom is seeing increasing adoption of cloud-native applications and AI projects in customers’ VCF-based private clouds for security, compliance, control and cost reasons.

Demand for object storage isn’t limited to the public cloud. The market for on-premises object storage is growing quickly, reflecting the strong demand for on-premises AI workloads.

VCF 9.1.2 Delivers Foundational Object Storage Capabilities

In VCF 9.1.2, vSAN introduces general availability of native S3-compatible object storage. It is the third storage type, alongside block and file, built directly into vSAN.

Because it runs natively in vSAN, the S3-compatible object storage inherits the scalability of any vSAN cluster. Teams scale up by adding capacity to existing hosts, or scale out by adding hosts, all without disruption.

Self-service multi-tenancy of vSAN native S3-compatible object storage through VCF Automation or vSphere Supervisor gives customers logical and physical isolation of buckets, with project-level isolation from day one. IT administrators can set access controls and quotas on buckets. The storage integrates with VCF features designed for multi-tenancy, including VPCs for networking isolation and VCF Automation constructs.

vSAN’s native object storage is secure. Because it is fully integrated, it takes advantage of the full stack of security capabilities of VCF. For instance, vSAN’s native object storage uses vSAN’s software-based encryption for data-at-rest and data-in-transit. It integrates with VCF features designed for security, such as VPCs for networking isolation.

A core set of S3 APIs is available at general availability for bucket and object operations, with an extensive roadmap to rapidly expand capabilities. Deployment and management run through the VCF Automation management plane, keeping operations simple for administrators.

vSAN S3-compatible object storage is easy to deploy, manage and consume, as it runs through the VCF Automation management plane.

Unlike competing object storage products that require separate purchases, separate management tooling and third-party automation software, vSAN native S3-compatible object storage is included with VCF licenses at no additional cost and is fully integrated with VMware Cloud Foundation for simplicity of deployment, scaling, management and consumption. Customers also save on operational costs by simplifying storage management onto a single platform.

Compared to cloud-based object storage, an on-premises approach can cost significantly less over time. Cloud providers charge for egress at nearly four times the storage rate itself. They also charge for API calls that compound with usage. For workloads that move data frequently, like AI training pipelines, these charges can push real-world cloud spend two to five times higher than raw storage rates.

Key Use Cases of vSAN Native Object Storage
In this release, vSAN native S3-compatible object storage is best suited to applications that manage their own data protection and versioning, such as build artifact repositories, Kubernetes backups, and Agentic AI.

DevOps. With VCF Automation, vSAN delivers S3 buckets-as-a-service for Kubernetes-orchestrated applications with self-provisioning and tenant isolation, reducing requirements for third-party tooling. We see two key use cases for vSAN native S3-compatible object storage in devops practices.

  • S3 Bucket-as-a-Build-Artifact Repository: Because vSAN’s native object storage is S3-compatible, it integrates with the most popular CI/CD tools on the market today used in DevOps. vSAN provisions storage faster than on-premises options, and it can scale incrementally, lowering your up-front storage costs. The net benefit is lower cost object storage that is already integrated with the infrastructure and applications you use today.
  • S3 Bucket-as-a-Kubernetes and Database Backup Repository: vSAN native object storage can be used easily for VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) and Data Services Manager (DSM) backup of data and persistent volumes without the need for third party tools.

Agentic AI: Agentic AI does not rely on a single data type, and it requires multiple storage protocols. vSAN provides block, file and S3-compatible object storage for agentic AI workloads on the same infrastructure with the same tool set. The raw, unstructured data is stored on vSAN object storage, then applications such as Tanzu Greenplum process and vectorize the data. Vector embeddings are stored on block storage, which deliver the performance required for instant similarity searches. Agentic AI models can be stored on vSAN native file shares, resulting in a high-performance AI engine all stored locally on VMware vSAN in VCF.

vSAN ESA delivers high-performance object storage that can meet the demands of agentic AI workloads by leveraging NVMe-based TLC. vSAN’s native S3-compatible object storage uses a proprietary zero-copy protocol developed internally that minimizes data processing through the storage stack, reducing I/O queuing and CPU overhead for fast performance. Object storage inherits vSAN’s native availability features, including fault domains and stretched clusters, so rack or site failures are handled without a separate protection layer . Finally, vSAN’s native snapshots allow teams to efficiently test their AI agents with cloned datasets without duplicating storage capacity or impacting production performance.

item.content:encoded:
For modern enterprise infrastructure, the primary focus has shifted from merely virtualizing compute to mastering unstructured data. With IDC forecasting global storage capacity to exceed 700 zettabytes by 2030, with nearly 80% of it unstructured, enterprise platform teams face an unsustainable paradox: developers and AI models expect the elastic, API-first consumption of public cloud, but data governance, low latency, predictability, and sovereign data residency mandate private infrastructure.

With the release of VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) 9.1.2, Broadcom bridges this gap. While the storage engine is natively powered by VMware vSAN, the breakthrough for cloud architects and platform engineers lies in how it is operationalized: native S3-compatible object storage delivered through centralized Service Management and consumed via VCF Automation.

Building directly on our companion blog, covering Centralized Service Management and Enterprise GitOps in VCF 9.1.2, this milestone transforms on-premises data architecture from an operations-heavy storage silo into an agile, developer-first cloud service.

Object Storage Fundamentals: Objects, Buckets, and the Universal S3 API

To understand why native private cloud S3 matters, consider the limitations of traditional storage. Block volumes (SAN) and hierarchical file trees (NAS) struggle when scaling to billions of unorganized data elements. Object storage replaces rigid directory hierarchies with a flat, infinitely expandable namespace built on three core pillars:

  • The Object: A discrete, self-contained unit comprising raw binary data, rich customizable metadata, and a globally unique identifier.
  • The Bucket: A logical, flat container that organizes objects across tenants without nested sub-directories.
  • The S3 API: The universal HTTP REST protocol (GET, PUT, DELETE, LIST) that has become the de facto interface for modern software, cloud services, and AI runtimes.

Historically, getting S3 endpoints meant turning to public hyperscalers like AWS S3 or standing up separate third-party appliances and software stacks such as MinIO, SeaweedFS, Dell ObjectScale, or NetApp StorageGRID. While functional, these introduced additional licensing, dedicated hardware requirements, and fragmented operational consoles.

VCF 9.1.2 changes the game: native S3 object storage now runs directly on your existing vSAN Express Storage Architecture (ESA) clusters at no extra software cost, turning your private cloud into a cloud-native service provider.

The Consumption Experience: Multi-Tenant S3 from Provider to Project

Delivering S3 as a private cloud service requires zero-touch developer velocity paired with rigorous provider guardrails. VCF Automation operationalizes this through a clear, multi-tiered consumption workflow:

1. The Provider Admin (Platform Infrastructure)

Operating within the VCF Automation Provider Portal, the Provider Admin configures the VMware vSphere Supervisor with the underlying vSAN Cluster in VMware vCenter. Through central Service Management, the admin installs the Object Store service across the regional fleet and assigns compute, zone/region quotas, and vSAN storage capacity to specific tenant organizations.

2. The Tenant/Org Admin (Organization Provisioning & Governance)

Within the VCF Automation Organization Portal, the Org Admin provisions dedicated or shared Object Store instances against their allocated capacity quotas. Crucially, following public cloud security conventions, all buckets are private by default. The Org Admin assigns tenant user access, defines fine-grained IAM and RBAC policies, and issues S3 service accounts and credentials mapped directly to enterprise identities.

3. The Project User (Application Teams & Data Scientists)

Without submitting IT tickets or waiting days for storage allocations, application developers and platform engineers log into the VCF Automation UI or use automated APIs. They create buckets on demand, manage objects, configure tags, and directly bind their S3 endpoints into application configurations.

Powering Production Use Cases: From Kubernetes Pipelines to Enterprise AI

This self-service model unlocks critical enterprise workloads across two domains:

1. DevOps and Cloud-Native Pipelines

Modern microservices rely heavily on ephemeral, highly available artifact repositories. With native S3 endpoints, automated CI/CD runners like Jenkins can upload build artifacts, binary packages, and container layers directly into self-provisioned buckets.

Furthermore, platform operators running VCF Automation can leverage tools like Velero via Data Protection with VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) Cluster Management. Velero points natively to local vSAN S3 buckets as its primary backup target, protecting container application state, namespaces, and persistent volume snapshots with local, wire-speed recovery without sending cluster metadata off-site.

2. Agentic AI and Enterprise Data Lakehouses

Autonomous AI agents require continuous ingestion and high-bandwidth retrieval of enterprise context. Housing unstructured corporate data (e.g., documents, transaction logs, communication archives) in native S3 buckets allows integrated query tools (such as VMware Tanzu Greenplum via PXF) to execute zero-copy analytics directly against Parquet or Iceberg datasets. This supports AI agents querying accurate corporate knowledge bases in real time without massive data movement.

The Sovereignty Imperative: Private Cloud vs. Public Cloud Economics

While public cloud S3 established the interface standard, running large-scale data lakes and AI pipelines in hyperscalers can introduce data egress costs, retrieval fees, and regulatory considerations.

Private S3 on VCF delivers substantial architectural advantages:

  • Data Sovereignty and Private AI: Models train and infer directly against corporate intellectual property inside your security perimeter. Sensitive data remains sovereign and strictly isolated, supported by private-by-default buckets and granular IAM and RBAC policies.
  • Air-Gapped Resiliency: Regulated industries, financial institutions, and defense environments can operate fully air-gapped, zero-trust cloud data lakes with no external cloud dependencies.
  • Predictable TCO: Removing the need for proprietary standalone storage appliances and third-party software licenses lowers total cost of ownership by up to 27% (based on Broadcom internal modeling), leveraging commodity server economics and integrated vSAN licensing.

Accelerate Your Private Cloud Evolution

The general availability of native vSAN S3 Object Storage in VCF 9.1.2 transforms VMware Cloud Foundation into a comprehensive data and automation platform. Block, file, and S3 object storage now share a unified control plane, delivering a public cloud-style consumption experience directly inside your private data center.

Ready to eliminate storage silos and deliver developer-ready S3 buckets on demand? Explore the technical documentation (Administering vSAN Object Storage and Using vSAN Object Storage) to begin consuming S3 services with VCF Automation today.

item.content:encoded:
As generative AI and AI agents redefine enterprise capabilities, organizations face a critical mandate to modernize their cloud infrastructure. With 56% of IT leaders running or planning to run production AI on private clouds*, the data center has become the strategic hub for next-generation innovation. However, attempting to support these advanced AI workloads with legacy infrastructure and manual processes creates an immediate bottleneck. To capitalize on this AI tipping point, IT organizations must deliver instant, self-service access to compute without compromising governance.

VCF 9.1.2 – What’s New in VCF Automation

The VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) 9.1.2 release tackles this challenge head-on by streamlining VCF Automation, the automated, self-service foundation of the VMware Private AI Cloud. By seamlessly unifying the delivery and lifecycle of private cloud services, VCF Automation empowers IT teams to act as cloud providers, helping developers and data scientists gain frictionless access to the infrastructure they need to build, run, and manage AI-driven applications.

Intelligent Service Management: The Central Engine for Fleet-Wide Control

Historically, managing the lifecycle of enterprise services across highly distributed infrastructure often involved routine administrative overhead. Provider Admins typically logged into individual VMware vCenter instances and regional Supervisors to deploy, track, and update services. While functional, this localized approach required extra engineering time to maintain consistent service states and manage configuration drift across the fleet. As environments expanded, coordinating service delivery across multiple regions without a centralized view could occasionally slow the pace of scaling new capabilities.

VCF Automation in VCF 9.1.2 resolves this by evolving Service Management into a fully unified, fleet-wide service delivery function. This update introduces the automated discovery of newly published service versions and provides a centralized inventory that seamlessly tracks deployed services and their valid upgrade paths. Provider Admins now possess single operational control to execute full service installs, upgrades, or uninstalls across their entire regional footprint from one centralized interface. This capability reduces administrative overhead and supports fleet-wide consistency, ultimately providing a public cloud-like operational experience on-premises.

Enterprise-Ready GitOps: Accelerating Continuous Delivery at Scale

Built directly upon this centralized Service Management foundation, the GitOps capability, powered by the Argo CD Service, transitions from Tech Preview to full General Availability in VCF 9.1.2. The GitOps with Argo CD Service achieves enterprise readiness through expanded scalability and a frictionless, out-of-the-box consumption model.

Initially administrators had to download the service from the Broadcom portal and manually upload it. Now, the GitOps Service is pre-bundled and available by default within the VCF Automation Provider Portal, reducing manual administrative overhead. The GA release also increases supported scale, comfortably accommodating the footprint of current enterprise deployments by supporting up to 200 namespaces for VCF Automation organizations. By leveraging native automated OpenID Connect (OIDC) identity integration and seamless attachment to target VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) clusters via Service Management, platform teams can establish centralized, fleet-wide GitOps pipelines. This translates to faster developer onboarding, the reduction of configuration drift, and a robust continuous delivery solution.

Closing the Gap with Public Cloud: Deploying Object Storage as a Service

To establish a self-service private cloud that delivers the agility and scale of the public cloud, organizations must offer robust, developer-ready storage services out-of-the-box. VCF 9.1.2 addresses this by marking the General Availability of the VMware vSAN S3 Compatible Object Storage.

The deployment and lifecycle management of this new S3 service is fully integrated into the enhanced Service Management framework. Instead of navigating disparate systems, Provider Admins can seamlessly deploy and upgrade the S3 Object Store Service alongside GitOps and Harbor using the same unified interface. This enables application and data science teams to consume S3-compatible object storage as a self-service Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) offering, accelerating the setup of complex AI and machine learning workloads without stalling innovation behind IT ticketing queues.

Driving Tangible ROI for Private AI Cloud

By centralizing the operational control plane through Service Management in VCF Automation, VCF 9.1.2 slashes the administrative overhead of managing distributed infrastructure and drives ROI. This fleet-wide control over GitOps and S3 Object Storage reclaims valuable engineering hours and mitigates configuration drift. Delivering robust continuous delivery and self-service storage out-of-the-box directly powers Day 0-2 operations for the VMware Private AI Cloud. Replacing manual ticketing with frictionless access equips developers and data scientists to fuel next-generation AI initiatives, reducing infrastructure delivery times and accelerating time-to-market.

Take the Next Step with VCF 9.1.2

Are you ready to transform your data center into a modern, multi-tenant private AI cloud? Explore how the unified service delivery of VCF 9.1.2 can accelerate your path to production. Check out the official VCF 9.1.2 release notes today for further details on how to operationalize your VMware Private AI Cloud with VCF Automation.
